subject: Heat Transfer
summary: Newton's law of cooling, the dimensionless numbers (Re, Pr, Nu, Gr, Ra, St), velocity and thermal boundary layers, laminar and turbulent flat-plate correlations, tube flow (entry length, Dittus–Boelter, fully developed Nu), free convection on vertical plates and the Reynolds–Colburn analogy
next_day: General Aptitude, Quant II & Data Interpretation

questions.text: The Nusselt number hL/k at a surface represents the ratio of
opts: heat conducted in the solid to heat convected by the fluid
convective heat transfer to the heat that would be conducted across a stagnant fluid layer of thickness L
questions.ans: (B) convective heat transfer to the heat that would be conducted across a stagnant fluid layer of thickness L
solution: Concept: Nu = hL/kf = (hΔT)/(kfΔT/L): convective heat flux divided by the pure-conduction flux through the same fluid layer.
Nu = 1 means the fluid is effectively stagnant (pure conduction); larger Nu means stronger convection.
Option (A) describes the Biot number, which uses k of the solid; (C) is Pr and (D) is Gr.
Exam tip: Nu and Bi look alike (hL/k). Nu uses the fluid's k, Bi uses the solid's k.

questions.text: Engine oil (ν = 1.0 × 10<sup>−4</sup> m²/s, Pr = 500) flows at 0.5 m/s through a 25 mm diameter tube. Using L<sub>h</sub> ≈ 0.05 Re D for the hydrodynamic entry length and L<sub>t</sub> ≈ L<sub>h</sub> Pr for the thermal entry length, the thermal entry length (in m, round off to one decimal place) is ______
solution: Concept: In laminar flow the entry lengths grow with Re; the thermal one is longer by the factor Pr.
Exam tip: For oils (Pr ≫ 1) the flow is thermally developing over almost any practical tube, so fully developed Nu = 3.66 underestimates h.

questions.text: Air at 4 m/s flows parallel to the 0.6 m side of a flat plate 0.6 m × 0.5 m, as shown. The plate is 60 °C hotter than the air. Air properties: ν = 1.5 × 10<sup>−5</sup> m²/s, k = 0.026 W/m·K, Pr = 0.71. Using Nu<sub>L</sub> = 0.664 Re<sub>L</sub><sup>1/2</sup> Pr<sup>1/3</sup>, the heat transfer rate from the top face (in W, round off to one decimal place) is ______
solution: Concept: Laminar flat plate (ReL < 5 × 105): average Nu = 0.664 ReL1/2 Pr1/3, with L measured along the flow.
Re<sub>L</sub> = 4 × 0.6/1.5 × 10<sup>−5</sup> = 1.6 × 10<sup>5</sup> (laminar)
Exam tip: The average h over 0 to L is twice the local h at x = L for laminar flow.

questions.text: The thermal boundary layer on a heated flat plate is thicker than the velocity boundary layer when
solution: Concept: δ/δt ≈ Pr1/3. Pr = ν/α compares how fast momentum and heat diffuse.
If Pr < 1 (gases ≈ 0.7, liquid metals ≈ 0.01), heat diffuses faster than momentum, so δ<sub>t</sub> > δ.
For oils and water (Pr > 1) the thermal layer is thinner.
Exam tip: Pr = 1 makes the two profiles identical: this is the basis of the Reynolds analogy.

questions.text: Air (k = 0.027 W/m·K, ν = 1.6 × 10<sup>−5</sup> m²/s, Pr = 0.7) flows at 10 m/s through a 50 mm diameter duct and is being cooled. Using the Dittus–Boelter equation Nu = 0.023 Re<sup>0.8</sup> Pr<sup>n</sup>, the heat transfer coefficient (in W/m²·K, round off to one decimal place) is ______
solution: Concept: Dittus–Boelter for fully developed turbulent flow (Re > 104): n = 0.4 when the fluid is heated, n = 0.3 when it is cooled.
Exam tip: In turbulent tube flow h ∝ u0.8/D0.2, so doubling the velocity raises h by 20.8 = 1.74.

questions.text: For hydrodynamically and thermally fully developed laminar flow in a circular tube with a uniform wall temperature, the Nusselt number based on diameter is
solution: Concept: In fully developed laminar flow both velocity and dimensionless temperature profiles stop changing, so Nu is a constant.
Uniform wall temperature: Nu = 3.66; uniform wall heat flux: Nu = 4.36.
Nu does not depend on Re or Pr once the flow is fully developed (laminar).
Exam tip: Since Nu is fixed, h = 3.66k/D: a smaller tube gives a larger h.

questions.text: Water (c<sub>p</sub> = 4180 J/kg·K) at 0.1 kg/s is heated from 20 °C to 60 °C in a 30 mm diameter tube whose wall supplies a uniform heat flux of 20 kW/m², as shown. The required tube length (in m, round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: Energy balance on the fluid: q″(πDL) = ṁcp(To − Ti). With uniform q″ the mean temperature rises linearly along the tube.
Surface needed: πDL = 16720/20000 = 0.836 m²
Exam tip: With uniform heat flux, Ts − Tm = q″/h stays constant in the fully developed region, so both lines are parallel.

questions.text: The Grashof number for a vertical plate of height L at temperature T<sub>s</sub> in a fluid at T<sub>∞</sub> is
solution: Concept: Gr = buoyancy force/viscous force = gβΔTL³/ν².
Option (D) is the Rayleigh number Ra = Gr Pr; option (C) is the Reynolds number.
For an ideal gas β = 1/T<sub>f</sub>, with T<sub>f</sub> the absolute film temperature.
Exam tip: Laminar-to-turbulent transition for a vertical plate occurs at Ra ≈ 109.

questions.text: A vertical plate 2 m high is at 100 °C in still air at 20 °C. Air properties at the film temperature: ν = 1.9 × 10<sup>−5</sup> m²/s, k = 0.029 W/m·K, Pr = 0.7, β = 1/333 K<sup>−1</sup>; g = 9.81 m/s². Using Nu<sub>L</sub> = 0.10 Ra<sub>L</sub><sup>1/3</sup> for turbulent flow, the average heat transfer coefficient (in W/m²·K, round off to two decimal places) is ______
solution: Concept: Free convection on a vertical plate: Ra = gβΔTL³Pr/ν²; turbulent when Ra > 109.
Exam tip: With the 1/3 power, L cancels: h in turbulent free convection does not depend on plate height.

questions.text: For laminar flow over a flat plate, if the free-stream velocity is doubled (all else unchanged), the average heat transfer coefficient becomes
solution: Concept: Laminar: NuL = 0.664 ReL1/2 Pr1/3, so h ∝ u1/2.
Doubling u multiplies h by 21/2 = 1.414.
Option (D) would apply to turbulent flow (h ∝ u<sup>0.8</sup>).
Exam tip: Remember the exponents: laminar 1/2, turbulent 0.8, natural laminar Ra1/4, natural turbulent Ra1/3.

questions.text: Air (ν = 1.6 × 10<sup>−5</sup> m²/s, k = 0.027 W/m·K, Pr = 0.7) flows at 30 m/s over a flat plate 2 m long whose boundary layer is tripped so that it is turbulent from the leading edge. Using Nu<sub>L</sub> = 0.037 Re<sub>L</sub><sup>0.8</sup> Pr<sup>1/3</sup>, the average heat transfer coefficient (in W/m²·K, round off to one decimal place) is ______
solution: Concept: For a fully turbulent boundary layer on a plate, local Nux = 0.0296 Rex0.8 Pr1/3; averaging over L gives 0.037 ReL0.8 Pr1/3.
Exam tip: If the first part of the plate is laminar, use the mixed form Nu = (0.037 Re0.8 − 871) Pr1/3.

questions.text: The velocity and thermal boundary layers on a flat plate have the same thickness when
solution: Concept: δ/δt = Pr1/3; the momentum and energy equations become identical in form when ν = α.
So δ = δt exactly when Pr = 1.
This similarity is what gives the Reynolds analogy St = C<sub>f</sub>/2.
Exam tip: Gases (Pr ≈ 0.7) come close, which is why the Reynolds/Colburn analogy works well for air.

questions.text: In laminar flow through a tube heated from the entrance, the local heat transfer coefficient along the tube
opts: is zero at the entrance and rises to a constant value
is constant along the whole tube
is highest near the entrance and decreases to a constant fully developed value
questions.ans: (C) is highest near the entrance and decreases to a constant fully developed value
solution: Concept: At the entrance the thermal boundary layer is very thin, so the temperature gradient at the wall (and h) is large.
As the thermal layer grows, h falls and settles at the fully developed value (Nu = 3.66 or 4.36).
So the average h of a short tube is higher than the fully developed value.
Exam tip: The same 'high near the start' behaviour is seen on a flat plate, where hx ∝ x−1/2.

questions.text: Air at 20 °C flows at 8 m/s across a long cylinder of 25 mm diameter whose surface is at 120 °C, as shown. Air properties: ν = 1.6 × 10<sup>−5</sup> m²/s, k = 0.027 W/m·K, Pr = 0.7. Using Nu<sub>D</sub> = 0.193 Re<sub>D</sub><sup>0.618</sup> Pr<sup>1/3</sup>, the heat loss per metre length of the cylinder (in W/m, round off to the nearest integer) is ______
solution: Concept: Cross-flow over a cylinder (Hilpert type): NuD = C ReDm Pr1/3, with C and m chosen for the Re range (here 4000 to 40 000).
Exam tip: The characteristic length for a cylinder in cross-flow is its diameter, not its length.

questions.text: A metal ball is cooled in an air stream. In calculating its Biot number and the Nusselt number of the air flow, the thermal conductivity used is
opts: that of the metal in both
that of the air in both
that of the metal for Bi and that of the air for Nu
that of the air for Bi and that of the metal for Nu
questions.ans: (C) that of the metal for Bi and that of the air for Nu
solution: Concept: Bi = hLc/ksolid compares conduction inside the solid with convection at its surface.
Nu = hD/k<sub>fluid</sub> is the dimensionless temperature gradient in the fluid at the wall.
So kmetal goes into Bi and kair into Nu: option (C).
Exam tip: For a sphere, Bi uses Lc = D/6 (lumped) while Nu uses D.
